# Bulk CSV inventory import

Author: Alex Callow
Date: 2026-11-26

## Overview

An inventory operator uploads inventory_frame.csv directly to S3 using a presigned URL. The BFF delegates job creation to Spring Boot, which records AWAITING_UPLOAD and assigns uploads/{jobId}/inventory_frame.csv. An S3-triggered Lambda sends the upload event to SQS. Spring Boot moves the job to PENDING and starts Temporal workflow csv-import-{jobId}. SQS retries failed delivery and a DLQ listener records dispatch failures.

The worker streams the CSV into job-scoped UNLOGGED PostgreSQL staging in batches and heartbeats during loading. It records invalid rows in import_row_errors and applies set-based writes with MERGE RETURNING where appropriate. The proposed six-table target and frame history must be reconciled with the repository's existing versioned schema. Inventory changes and outbox records must commit together.

## Agreed import behavior

- A newer source timestamp creates a version. An equal timestamp and matching content hash is a no-op. An older timestamp produces STALE_RECORD. An equal timestamp with different content produces TIMESTAMP_COLLISION_CONFLICT and records both hashes. Skipped conflicts result in COMPLETED_WITH_ERRORS.
- The explicit forceOverwrite flag accepts stale and same-timestamp conflicts. The new version preserves source_modified_date and records FORCED_OVERWRITE and import_job_id. Close and open at one database-generated boundary strictly later than the locked current valid_from.
- DELTA is the default and leaves absent frames alone. FULL_SNAPSHOT requires an explicit GLOBAL scope or validated partition scope using country, region or environment. Every identifiable frame ID in the file counts as present, including rows with invalid payloads.
- FULL_SNAPSHOT soft-retires absent active frames in scope with MISSING_FROM_FULL_SNAPSHOT. Abort if more than 10% of scoped active frames would retire. A malformed-row rate above 5% must prevent retirement. Whether to fail the whole snapshot is open.

## Analysis

All seven Goldfish lenses completed review. The recommendations below are proposed decisions for RFC alignment.

### Delivery and recovery

- Bind each job to one immutable object. Sign the exact key and the create-only PUT condition (If-None-Match: *), enable S3 versioning, and persist the accepted version ID so every retry reads the same bytes. Keep the object through the retry and reconciliation window. Validate the bucket, decoded key, object version, and size before dispatch. [S3 conditional writes](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/conditional-writes.html) [S3 event delivery](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/notification-how-to-event-types-and-destinations.html)
- Record PENDING conditionally, invoke Temporal with the job-derived workflow ID, and acknowledge SQS only after start or after confirming the same job's workflow already exists. Configure both running-ID conflict and closed-ID reuse policies. A crash between the DB write and Temporal start leaves a retryable PENDING job. A lost start response must be reconciled before any DLQ transition to FAILED. Guard terminal states and fence a late starter with conditional job transitions before it can apply inventory. Reconcile old AWAITING_UPLOAD and PENDING jobs against S3 and Temporal, and cover Lambda delivery failures separately from consumer DLQ failures. [Temporal workflow ID policies](https://docs.temporal.io/develop/java/nexus/development-walkthrough/send-messages)
- Stage by job ID, attempt generation, and logical CSV row number. Record observed frame IDs independently of row validity. Mark a generation complete only after EOF and verify that its completion marker and counts still match before applying. Keep the marker in unlogged storage with the staged rows so recovery clears both, and reload from the bound S3 version when the marker is missing. Use heartbeats for liveness and cancellation. Restart the stream for an incomplete generation in the first release. Record row errors durably with stable keys so retries do not duplicate errors. [PostgreSQL unlogged tables](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/sql-createtable.html)

### Inventory apply

- Reuse the existing stable-frame lock, current-version uniqueness constraint, and close-and-append history. The repository already computes a boundary as the greater of database wall-clock time and the current valid_from plus one microsecond, then uses that boundary for the next version. Reuse this rule for all imported changes, including retirements. Preserve source_modified_at separately. The existing schema already stores versioned external references and links. Map each of the 45 CSV fields before adding new tables or moving attributes. Keep immutable history when normalizing shared site or spec data. [Schema](../frame-inventory-schema/frame-inventory-schema.md) [Repository](../../src/backend/src/main/java/com/global/ct/frameinventory/frame/FrameRepository.java)
- Define the content hash over canonical typed values, including versioned links and external references. Specify normalization, timezone and precision, null behavior, and duplicate-ID handling. Change manual UI/API writes to set source_modified_at from statement_timestamp() on the version insert after obtaining the frame lock. Preserve the source timestamp on CSV imports, including forced overwrites. Define how comparisons handle legacy manual versions that inherited an older source timestamp. A forced overwrite can move the current source timestamp backward. A separate source high-water mark remains an open decision.
- Build one candidate per target key before set-based writes. Resolve shared dimensions and reserve frame identities before opening dependent versions and links. PostgreSQL 18 supports MERGE RETURNING, but a source candidate takes only one action, so close and append in separate set-based statements in the same transaction. Use the actual changed version IDs to produce outbox records. Commit versions, links, outbox, and final job status together. A retry after a lost commit response returns the committed result. [PostgreSQL MERGE](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/sql-merge.html)
- Compute the retirement numerator and denominator on the same protected pre-apply inventory view. Row locks protect existing IDs, while new frames and edits that move into or out of scope require a shared writer protocol. Start with a transaction-scoped inventory lock held in shared mode by manual writes and DELTA applies, and in exclusive mode by snapshots. Take per-frame locks in stable ID order. This serializes promotion of snapshots even when their scopes are disjoint. Keep it out of upload, parsing, and staging. Measure lock time before enabling the feature. Never infer absence from a partial stream or an unrecoverable CSV parse error. Decide whether unidentifiable rows, scope violations, and header-only snapshots fail the whole job. The proposed default is to fail a snapshot before any inventory write when a safety check fails.

### Snapshot watermark

- Persist snapshot_as_of on the job. Accept a producer-supplied export watermark at job creation. When omitted, derive it from MAX(modified_date) after scanning the complete file. Use one documented source timezone and precision for comparisons. Require the exporter to supply an explicit watermark when the file cannot establish one. MAX(modified_date) measures the newest row change and can lag the time a complete export was generated. It also cannot prove completeness, so prefer the explicit export watermark for feeds where these times differ.
- Use canonical scope keys in a containment hierarchy: GLOBAL, country, country/region, and country/region/environment. Require a region for every environment-level FULL_SNAPSHOT in the first release. Reject a country/environment scope such as UK/UNDERGROUND at job creation. An operator can export a separate authoritative snapshot for each region or use DELTA for a cross-region file.
- Before inventory writes and under the snapshot apply lock, reject a watermark outside the freshness window (proposed default 24 hours), in the future beyond allowed clock skew, or strictly below the maximum committed watermark for the requested scope and its ancestors. Equal watermarks pass this check. On successful commit, advance only the requested scope's watermark, including when the job completes with row errors. A failed job leaves all watermarks as they were.
- A newer descendant watermark does not reject an enclosing snapshot. Apply normal row conflict checks throughout the requested scope, including newer child scopes. Before retiring absent frames, exclude the entire subtree of each descendant whose committed watermark is strictly newer than the incoming watermark. Report the protected scopes and skipped retirement count. A descendant at the same watermark remains eligible. For example, a GLOBAL export at 11:30 can apply after a partition snapshot at 12:00, with retirement excluded in that partition. A partition export at 11:00 fails if an ancestor already committed at 12:00.
- Among the remaining absent active frames, exclude any whose current valid_from or source_modified_at is after snapshot_as_of and record SKIPPED_RETIREMENT_NEWER_THAN_SNAPSHOT. This protects newer current versions, including edits within the same scope. Count only eligible retirements in the 10% numerator and keep the denominator as all pre-apply active frames in the declared scope. Capture the watermark checks, both exclusion counts, the breaker calculation, and the scope watermark update in the same protected apply transaction.

### Snapshot history and reactivation

The agreed representation is a new current version with status RETIRED and reason MISSING_FROM_FULL_SNAPSHOT. Define how current inventory queries treat that version and how a later import reactivates it. Existing manual deletion closes the last current version without opening a replacement. Keep those behaviors explicit in the status and history contract. If snapshot closure sets closed_by_change_source, extend the V2 constraint, which currently allows only MANUAL_DELETE. [V2 migration](../../src/backend/src/main/resources/db/migration/V2__add_frame_change_source.sql)

## Goals and non-goals

- Deliver authenticated upload, visible job progress and row errors, retry-safe imports, audited versions, scoped retirement, and transactional outbox records.
- Leave mass deletion, generalized CSV mapping, automatic repair of malformed source values, and multi-scope FULL_SNAPSHOT uploads outside the first release. If authoritative cross-region exports become a regular need, consider one atomic job over explicitly named scopes, each with its own watermark and retirement check.

## Alternatives weighed

- Keep the S3-to-Lambda bridge as requested. Direct S3-to-SQS delivery could remove an operational failure path if the bridge only forwards events. Verify what routing or event normalization the Lambda needs to own.
- Keep UNLOGGED staging with full source replay for initial implementation. Durable staging could reduce replay cost and operational complexity after failover, at the cost of logging intermediate data. Benchmark with the expected maximum file.
- Reuse versioned history as the initial design direction. Add a separate frame_history table only if it serves a distinct audited need. Otherwise two history stores would require agreement on which is authoritative.

## Key decisions and implementation sequence

1. Map the CSV to the current schema and the proposed six entities. Resolve source timestamp parsing, manual-edit ordering, force authorization, link semantics, duplicate IDs, and schema ownership before migrations.
2. Add durable job, row error, lineage, and outbox storage through additive Flyway migrations. Expose BFF job creation and status, including counts, fatal errors, and paginated row errors. Set upload-size, row-count, timeout, and retention limits from the agreed operating envelope.
3. Implement the S3 event bridge, SQS dispatch and DLQ, and Temporal start. Exercise duplicate notifications, late events, ambiguous starts, and reconciliation before applying inventory.
4. Implement staging and atomic DELTA apply. Run the supplied CSV against PostgreSQL 18 and check replay, timestamp collisions, manual edits, forced overwrite, malformed quoting, duplicate IDs, lost staging, and worker failure immediately after commit.
5. Add scoped FULL_SNAPSHOT with a protected retirement calculation. Verify that malformed rows with IDs stay present, out-of-scope frames stay untouched, and the exact 5% and 10% boundaries behave as agreed. Exercise rejection of environment scopes without a region, expired and out-of-order watermarks, watermark equality, derived watermarks, newer ancestors rejecting narrower snapshots, newer descendants protecting entire subtrees while present rows still upsert, frames created or moved into scope after export, and concurrent manual writes. Roll out DELTA first, then enable snapshot after observing apply times and reviewing operator safeguards.
6. Track queue age and DLQ depth, time in each job state, staging retries, apply transaction duration, row error codes, retirement guard trips, and outbox lag. Correlate logs by job ID and keep presigned URLs and raw row content out of logs.
# Frame inventory schema and version history

- **Author** Alex Callow
- **Date** 2026-11-26

## Overview

PostgreSQL stores a stable `frame_id` for each frame and a separate row for each accepted version. The [Flyway migration](../../src/backend/src/main/resources/db/migration/V1__create_frame_inventory.sql) creates the empty inventory tables on Spring Boot startup.

The supplied extract contains 1,000 rows, 1,000 distinct frame IDs, and 45 fields. The exercise calls for a user-driven import. [CSV](../../data/inventory_frame.csv) [Exercise requirements](../../INSTRUCTIONS.md#L52-L64)

## CSV field mapping

CSV values arrive as text. A blank optional value becomes SQL `NULL`. Counts and value sets describe the supplied extract.

| CSV fields | Observed representation | PostgreSQL mapping |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `frame_id` | Ten decimal digits, unique and populated in all rows | `frame.frame_id text` primary key. The prototype also uses alphanumeric frame IDs. |
| `created_date`, `modified_date` | Date and time to seconds, without offsets | `frame_version.source_created_at` and `source_modified_at`, both `timestamp without time zone`. |
| `country_code`, `region`, `town` | Codes and names. One country, 12 regions, 172 towns | Country code and region name form the region's natural key. Town name is scoped to a region. Each table also has a generated primary key. |
| `postcode` | UK postcode with a space, 484 distinct | `postcode` row keyed by generated ID, unique on `(town_id, postcode)`. |
| `postcode_area`, `postcode_district`, `postcode_sector`, `postcode_unit` | Text fragments, some containing letters | Derive from the postcode. The four fragments reconstruct it exactly in all 1,000 rows. |
| `longitude`, `latitude` | Signed decimal degrees | Exact `numeric` columns on `frame_version`, with valid coordinate ranges. |
| `location` | `POINT (latitude longitude)` text | Derive from the scalar coordinates if an export requires the legacy format. All 1,000 rows contain the same pair in this order. |
| `site_no`, `inventory_site_no`, `panel_number` | Identifiers. Site and panel numbers can contain leading zeros | Independent `text` fields on `frame_version`. |
| `location_id` | Identifier, 13 blanks | Nullable `text` on `frame_version`. In 67 rows the populated value differs from the normalized postcode. |
| `environment`, `address`, `station`, `airport` | Text. Station has 593 blanks and airport has 887 | `text` on `frame_version`, with the optional site names nullable. |
| `type_classic_digital`, `format`, `size_group_code` | Codes. Nine distinct combinations | `frame_format` row keyed by generated ID, unique on the three codes. Codes stay as text, including size groups such as `006`. |
| `size_code`, `aspect_ratio_code`, `t_size` | Codes and labels. `t_size` has 57 blanks | `text` columns on `frame_version`. |
| `pixel_height`, `pixel_width` | Positive integers, 28 blanks in each column | Nullable `integer` dimensions on `frame_version`. |
| `illumination_type_id`, `number_of_slots`, `distance_to_closest_school` | Integer code, count, and distance | `integer` on `frame_version`. The distance is assumed to be in metres, consistent with the prototype. |
| `status`, `status_reason` | Text. Every row is `LIVE` and all reasons are blank | Status and nullable reason on `frame_version`. |
| `impact_weight` | Decimal, six blanks | Nullable exact `numeric` on `frame_version`. |
| `premium` | `0` or `1` | `boolean` on `frame_version`. |
| `production_rate_card`, `production_rate_card_legacy` | Both columns are blank throughout | Separate nullable `text` fields until the source contract establishes how they relate. |
| `pricing_grade` | Text, 869 blanks | Nullable `text` on `frame_version`. |
| `price_entity_id`, `broadsign_display_unit_id`, `broadsign_frame_id`, `broadsign_domain_id` | Opaque codes. Broadsign fields have 3, 979, and 29 blanks respectively | `frame_version_external_reference` rows keyed by `(version_id, reference_type)`, with identifier values as text. Values can recur across frames. |
| `linked_frame_ids` | Comma-separated IDs, present in four rows | Ordered `frame_version_link` rows keyed by `(version_id, position)`, with each target ID as text. Each supplied list includes its source frame and a peer. |

## Relational structure

- `frame_version` has a primary key and foreign keys to `frame`, `postcode`, and `frame_format`. `postcode` references `town`, which references `region`. When lookup values change, the writer creates or reuses a row with the new values so earlier versions keep their original values.
- External references and linked frame IDs belong to the version that carried them. Both child tables reference that version. Resolve a linked target by joining its source ID to `frame.frame_id`. This lets a partial upload preserve a reference before its target arrives.
- Keep address, position, and coordinates on the version. Eight `site_no` values map to multiple `inventory_site_no` values, and 95 `inventory_site_no` values map to multiple `site_no` values. Even matching pairs can have different coordinates and addresses.
- Store format and size-group codes independently in the format tuple. Their values line up one-to-one in this extract. A wider export may contain combinations absent here. Status, technology, and slot count also vary in the intended product even though each is uniform in this sample.

## Versioning contract

| Incoming CSV row | Result |
| --- | --- |
| First row for a frame | Insert the stable frame and its first current version. |
| Strictly older source `modified_date` | Leave the current row, links, and history as they were. |
| Equal or newer source `modified_date` | Set the old row's `is_current` to false and its `valid_to` to the transition instant. Insert a current version with `valid_from` set to that same instant. |

The migration uses `timestamptz` for half-open validity intervals `[valid_from, valid_to)`. Check constraints require a positive interval for closed versions and tie `is_current` to whether `valid_to` is null. A partial unique index enforces at most one current version per frame.

The future CSV upload, create, and edit paths will share a Spring `@Transactional` service. The service creates or locks the stable frame row before comparing source timestamps. It closes the current version and appends its replacement in the same transaction. The transition time must be later than the previous version's start, including when two rows are accepted in one transaction.

Source timestamps retain their original wall-clock values. Equal timestamps append a new version, including when the same file is uploaded again. Manual creation can start with null source timestamps. Manual edits carry forward the last accepted source timestamp. History starts with the first accepted version because the CSV contains one snapshot per frame.

## Alternatives weighed

- One wide mutable row has a simple current read and loses revisions. A second mutable current table would duplicate the version data and require another write on each transition. Index the current versions in the history table.
- One table per category code would add joins and introduce catalog rules that the extract cannot establish. Share the repeated region, town, postcode, and format tuples and keep frame-specific values with each historical version.
- A foreign key from each linked target to an existing frame gives immediate referential integrity and forces partial uploads to wait for every target. Preserve each source target identifier and enforce the owner foreign key. An unresolved target can join to its frame once that frame arrives.

## Scope and verification

Flyway V1 defines the tables, keys, validity checks, and indexes. CSV parsing, the shared write service, and the upload, edit, and history screens are future application work.

Flyway applied V1 on PostgreSQL 18.6 and skipped it on restart. A rollback-only check loaded all 1,000 CSV rows and exercised the database constraints. The [backend README](../../src/backend/README.md) describes how to verify the migration using `flyway_schema_history`.

Spring gRPC serves frame management on port 9090. Spring MVC and Actuator serve health endpoints on port 8080. Spring Boot applies Flyway migrations against PostgreSQL at startup. The Docker image builds a Spring Boot JAR and runs it on Java 21. [build.gradle:languageVersion] [build.gradle:dependencies] [Dockerfile:RUN] [Dockerfile:ENTRYPOINT] ## Subdirectories & Boundaries - [Source tree](./src/README.md) contains the application and its runtime configuration. - [Inventory migration](./src/main/resources/db/migration/V1__create_frame_inventory.sql) creates the frame, version history, and related tables. - [Frame inventory schema](../../docs/frame-inventory-schema/frame-inventory-schema.md) maps the CSV fields and describes the shared Spring write transaction. ## Local development Start the Compose PostgreSQL service from the repository root with `docker compose up -d --wait postgres`. From `src/backend`, run `./gradlew bootRun` with Java 21. The local JDBC defaults connect to the Compose database. Set `SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL`, `SPRING_DATASOURCE_USERNAME`, and `SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD` when connecting to a different database. ## Verification From `src/backend`, run `./gradlew test` with Java 21 and Docker available. The suite covers unit tests and calls the gRPC service through a generated client against PostgreSQL 18.6 using Testcontainers. Flyway applies both schema migrations during the integration tests. ## Frame management API The [Protobuf definition](src/main/proto/frameinventory/v1/frames.proto) declares the six RPCs. Run `./gradlew generateProto` to generate the Java messages and stubs. The [API contract](../../docs/frame-management-grpc-api.md#grpc-contract) describes pagination, request fields, errors, and version checks. With the backend running, call the service from `src/backend` using `grpcurl`. ```sh grpcurl -plaintext -import-path src/main/proto -proto frameinventory/v1/frames.proto \ -d '{"page":0,"size":25}' localhost:9090 frameinventory.v1.FrameManagement/ListFrames ``` The backend writes structured JSON logs to the console. Set `LOGGING_LEVEL_COM_GLOBAL_CT_FRAMEINVENTORY_FRAME=DEBUG` to include frame RPC parameters, version checks, lookup results, and handled client errors. ## Sentry error reporting Set `SENTRY_DSN` to the DSN of the backend's Sentry project and set `SENTRY_ENVIRONMENT` to the environment name, such as `staging`. The environment defaults to `local`. An empty or unset DSN disables error reporting. Export the variables before running `./gradlew bootRun` from `src/backend`. For Docker Compose, export the same variables or set them in an untracked `.env` file at the repository root, then run `docker compose up --build -d backend` to rebuild and apply the settings. To verify reporting, use a non-production Sentry project or environment. In a local checkout, temporarily make a controller handler throw an `IllegalStateException` with a unique test message and call that route. Confirm the event appears in Sentry with the expected stack trace and environment tag, then link the event on the issue. Remove the temporary exception and confirm `curl --fail http://localhost:8080/api/health` succeeds with the DSN configured and again after restarting the backend with the DSN unset. # Frame Inventory Monorepo scaffold for the frame-inventory take-home exercise. ## System Overview The Next.js page calls the Spring Boot health endpoint through a same-origin rewrite. Docker Compose runs both modules alongside PostgreSQL, OpenSearch, OpenSearch Dashboards, Prometheus, Grafana, Loki, Alloy, and the OpenTelemetry Collector. The exercise provides a legacy export in `data/inventory_frame.csv` and describes the inventory features in `INSTRUCTIONS.md`. Bring the whole stack up with one command. ```bash docker compose up --build ``` Once PostgreSQL is healthy, the backend applies pending Flyway migrations during startup. If you have `just` installed, run `just` to list the available recipes. | Command | Purpose | |---------|---------| | `just up` | Build and start the whole stack in the foreground. | | `just down` | Stop the stack and retain its named data volumes. | | `just compose logs -f backend` | Pass arguments through to Docker Compose. | | `just migrate` | Run Flyway on its own in a one-off backend container. | ## Subdirectories & System Boundaries - [Application source](./src/README.md) contains the Spring Boot backend, Apollo Server BFF, and Next.js frontend. - [Design system](./design-system/README.md) contains the prototype, sample frame data, and visual conventions for the exercise. ## Services `docker compose up` starts the following services. | Service | Host port | Container port | Notes | |-----------------------|-----------|----------------|--------------------------------------------------------| | frontend | 3000 | 3000 | Next.js dev server, proxies `/api` to the backend | | bff | 4000 | 4000 | Apollo Sandbox and the frame inventory GraphQL API | | backend | 8080 | 8080 | Spring Boot, exposes `GET /api/health` | | postgres | 5432 | 5432 | Spring Boot applies the inventory schema via Flyway | | opensearch | 9200, 9600 | 9200, 9600 | Single-node, security plugin disabled for local use | | opensearch-dashboards | 5601 | 5601 | UI for the OpenSearch cluster above | | prometheus | 9091 | 9090 | Scrapes Spring Boot and Apollo metrics every 15 seconds | | otel-collector | 9464 | 9464 | Scrapes Spring Boot metrics for local inspection | | grafana | 3001 | 3000 | Queries provisioned Prometheus and Loki data | ### Credentials | Service | User | Password | Database | |-----------------------|------------|----------------|------------------| | postgres | `app` | `app` | `frames` | | opensearch | n/a | n/a | n/a | | grafana | `admin` | `admin` | n/a | ## Global Invariants - The Next.js rewrite preserves the `/api/` path and uses `BACKEND_URL` as its destination origin. Compose sets it to `http://backend:8080`. `[src/frontend/next.config.ts:rewrites]` `[docker-compose.yml:services.frontend.environment.BACKEND_URL]` - The health page expects `status`, `service`, and `timestamp` from `GET /api/health`. The backend supplies those fields directly. `[src/frontend/src/app/page.tsx:HealthResponse]` `[src/backend/src/main/java/com/global/ct/frameinventory/HealthController.java:health]` ## Global Side Effects - Opening the frontend requests `/api/health`, which the Next.js server forwards to the backend. The response reports the current time from the backend clock. `[src/frontend/src/app/page.tsx:Home]` `[src/frontend/next.config.ts:rewrites]` `[src/backend/src/main/java/com/global/ct/frameinventory/HealthController.java:health]` - Docker Compose publishes service ports and creates named volumes for PostgreSQL and OpenSearch. OpenSearch Dashboards connects to OpenSearch on the Compose network. `[docker-compose.yml:services]` `[docker-compose.yml:volumes]` `[docker-compose.yml:services.opensearch-dashboards.environment.OPENSEARCH_HOSTS]` ## System Verification - From `src/backend`, run `./gradlew test`. - From `src/frontend`, run `npm run lint` after installing dependencies. ### Git hooks Install [pre-commit](https://pre-commit.com/#installation), then run `pre-commit install` from the repository root to install both Git hooks. The `pre-commit` hook checks YAML, JSON, and merge conflict markers, and runs ESLint when staged changes touch `src/frontend/`. Install the frontend dependencies with `npm ci --prefix src/frontend` before committing frontend changes. The `commit-msg` hook uses Commitlint to enforce the Conventional Commits format documented in [AGENTS.md](./AGENTS.md). Commitlint requires Node.js 22.12 or newer. Run `pre-commit run --all-files` to check the whole repository. ### Smoke test Once the stack is up, check the service entry points. - Open — the page calls `/api/health` and prints the JSON response. - Hit the backend directly: . - Open [Apollo Sandbox](http://127.0.0.1:4000) and run the [frame list query](./src/bff/README.md). ### Backend metrics - Open [Prometheus Targets](http://127.0.0.1:9091/targets) and wait for the `frame-inventory-backend` target to show **UP**. It scrapes `http://backend:8080/actuator/prometheus` on the Compose network. - Open [Grafana](http://127.0.0.1:3001), sign in with the initial credentials above, and run `up{job="frame-inventory-backend"}` in **Explore** using the default Prometheus data source. A value of `1` confirms the backend is being scraped. - Open [Frame Inventory Backend](http://127.0.0.1:3001/d/frame-inventory-backend/frame-inventory-backend) for HTTP and gRPC request rate, errors, p50, p95, and p99 latency, and resource saturation. Generate API traffic and allow at least two Prometheus scrapes for request graphs to populate. - The **Frame inventory activity** section shows committed creates, updates, and soft deletes, plus successful gRPC reads and version conflicts. The totals cover the dashboard time range. Rejected or rolled-back writes and repeated deletes that change no data are excluded from the totals. Prometheus and Grafana listen on localhost. Their named volumes keep metrics and Grafana settings across restarts. ### BFF metrics Run `docker compose up -d --build bff prometheus grafana`. If Prometheus was already running, reload its scrape configuration with `docker compose restart prometheus`. Confirm that `frame-inventory-bff` is **UP** in [Prometheus Targets](http://127.0.0.1:9091/targets). Prometheus scrapes `http://bff:9465/metrics` on the Compose network. Open [Frame Inventory BFF](http://127.0.0.1:3001/d/frame-inventory-bff/frame-inventory-bff) for GraphQL request rate, error percentage, p50/p95/p99 latency, in-flight requests, and event loop utilization. The **Slowest queries and mutations (p95)** panel ranks top-level fields such as `frames` and `updateFrame` by resolver latency over the selected time range. Run the [frame list query](./src/bff/README.md) several times across at least two scrapes. Run `{ frames(page: -1) { page } }` to generate a GraphQL error. The dashboard counts GraphQL errors even when Apollo responds with HTTP 200. ### Backend and BFF logs Run `docker compose up -d --build bff grafana`. Alloy reads the backend and BFF containers’ stdout and stderr through the Docker socket and sends them to Loki. Loki stores logs in the `loki-data` volume with seven-day retention. For a failed GraphQL request, take the `X-Correlation-Id` response header and search both services with `{service_name=~"backend|bff"} | json | correlationId="your-id"`. For a production deployment, configure log storage, retention, and access controls for that environment. Open [Grafana Explore](http://127.0.0.1:3001/explore), select **Loki**, and switch to **Code** mode to run either LogQL query. - Backend — `{service_name="backend"}` - BFF — `{service_name="bff"}` ### OpenTelemetry Collector Run `docker compose up -d --build otel-collector` to start the Collector and its dependencies. The Collector scrapes `http://backend:8080/actuator/prometheus` every 15 seconds and exposes the latest samples on localhost. Introduction
Section titled “Introduction”
When you’re developing cloud and serverless applications, you need to grant access to various AWS resources like S3 buckets and RDS databases.
To handle this, you create IAM roles and assign permissions through policies.
However, configuring these policies can be challenging, especially if you want to ensure minimal access of all principals to your resources.
LocalStack IAM Policy Stream automates the generation of IAM policies for your AWS API requests on your local machine.
This stream helps you identify the necessary permissions for your cloud application and allows you to detect logical errors, such as unexpected actions in your policies.
This tutorial will guide you through setting up IAM Policy Stream for a locally running AWS application.
We’ll use a basic example involving an S3 bucket, an SQS queue, and a bucket notification configuration.
You’ll generate the policy for the bucket notification configuration and insert it into the SQS queue.
Why use IAM Policy Stream?
Section titled “Why use IAM Policy Stream?”
LocalStack enables you to create and enforce local IAM roles and policies using the ENFORCE_IAM feature.
However, users often struggle to figure out the necessary permissions for different actions.
It’s important to find a balance, avoiding giving too many permissions while making sure the right ones are granted.
This challenge becomes more complex when dealing with AWS services that make requests not directly visible to users.
For instance, if an SNS topic sends a message to an SQS queue and the underlying call fails, there might be no clear error message, causing confusion, especially for those less familiar with the services.
IAM Policy Stream simplifies this by automatically generating the needed policies and showing them to users.
This makes it easier to integrate with resources, roles, and users, streamlining the development process.
Additionally, it serves as a useful learning tool, helping users understand the permissions linked to various AWS calls and improving the onboarding experience for newcomers to AWS.
Prerequisites
Section titled “Prerequisites”
lstk with LOCALSTACK_AUTH_TOKEN
Docker
Terraform & lstk terraform
AWS CLI with lstk aws
LocalStack account
jq
Architecture diagram
Section titled “Architecture diagram”
The following diagram illustrates the architecture of this tutorial:
In this architecture:
An S3 bucket is configured to send event notifications when objects are created
An SQS queue receives these notifications
The IAM Enforcement Engine intercepts API calls and checks for proper permissions
The IAM Policy Stream Dashboard captures all API requests and generates the necessary IAM policies
When a file is uploaded to the S3 bucket, S3 attempts to send a message to SQS, which initially fails due to missing permissions
The IAM Policy Stream automatically generates the required policy, which can then be applied to resolve the violation
Tutorial: Configure an S3 bucket for event notifications using SQS
Section titled “Tutorial: Configure an S3 bucket for event notifications using SQS”
In this tutorial, you will configure a LocalStack S3 bucket to send event notifications to an SQS queue.
You will then use IAM Policy Stream to generate the necessary IAM policy for the SQS queue.
You will use Terraform to create the resources and the AWS CLI to interact with them.
With LocalStack’s IAM enforcement enabled, you can thoroughly test your policy and ensure that the development setup mirrors the production environment.
Start your LocalStack container
Section titled “Start your LocalStack container”
Launch the LocalStack container on your local machine using the specified command:
Terminal window
LOCALSTACK_DEBUG=1 LOCALSTACK_IAM_SOFT_MODE=1 lstk start
In the above command:
LOCALSTACK_DEBUG=1 turns on detailed logging to check API calls and IAM violations.
LOCALSTACK_IAM_SOFT_MODE=1 lets you test IAM enforcement by logging violations without stopping the API calls.
Create the Terraform configuration
Section titled “Create the Terraform configuration”
Create a new file called main.tf for the Terraform setup of an S3 bucket and an SQS queue.
Start by using the aws_sqs_queue resource to create an SQS queue named s3-event-notification-queue.
resource "aws_sqs_queue" "queue" {
name = "s3-event-notification-queue"
}
Next, use the aws_s3_bucket resource to create an S3 bucket called s3-event-notification-bucket.
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "bucket" {
bucket = "s3-event-notification-bucket"
}
Finally, use the aws_s3_bucket_notification resource to link the S3 bucket with the SQS queue for sending notifications:
resource "aws_s3_bucket_notification" "bucket_notification" {
bucket = aws_s3_bucket.bucket.id
queue {
queue_arn = aws_sqs_queue.queue.arn
events = ["s3:ObjectCreated:*"]
}
}
Deploy the Terraform configuration
Section titled “Deploy the Terraform configuration”
You can use lstk terraform to deploy your Terraform configuration within the LocalStack environment.
Run the following commands to initialize and apply the Terraform configuration:
Terminal window
lstk terraform init
lstk terraform apply
You will be prompted to confirm the changes.
Type yes to continue.
Since LocalStack is used, no real AWS resources are created.
LocalStack will emulate ephemeral development resources that will be removed automatically once you stop the LocalStack container.
After applying the Terraform configuration, the output will appear similar to this:
Terminal window
aws_sqs_queue.queue: Creating...
aws_s3_bucket.bucket: Creating...
aws_s3_bucket.bucket: Creation complete after 1s [id=s3-event-notification-bucket]
aws_sqs_queue.queue: Still creating... [10s elapsed]
aws_sqs_queue.queue: Still creating... [20s elapsed]
aws_sqs_queue.queue: Creation complete after 26s [id=http://sqs.us-east-1.localhost.localstack.cloud:4566/000000000000/s3-event-notification-queue]
aws_s3_bucket_notification.bucket_notification: Creating...
aws_s3_bucket_notification.bucket_notification: Creation complete after 0s [id=s3-event-notification-bucket]
Apply complete! Resources: 3 added, 0 changed, 0 destroyed.
Start the IAM Policy Stream
Section titled “Start the IAM Policy Stream”
Access the LocalStack Web Application and go to the IAM Policy Stream dashboard.
This feature enables you to directly examine the generated policies, displaying the precise permissions required for each API call.
You’ll observe the Stream active status icon, indicating that making any local AWS API request will trigger the generation of an IAM Policy.
Now, let’s proceed to upload a file to the S3 bucket to trigger the event notification and generate the IAM policy.
Trigger the event notification
Section titled “Trigger the event notification”
Create a new file named some-log-file.log and upload it to the S3 bucket using the AWS CLI:
Terminal window
echo "Hello, LocalStack" > some-log-file.log
lstk aws s3 cp some-log-file.log s3://s3-event-notification-bucket/
Uploading a file will activate an event notification, sending a message to the SQS queue.
However, since the SQS queue lacks the necessary permissions, an IAM violation will appear in the IAM Policy Stream dashboard.
You can also navigate to the LocalStack logs and observe the IAM violation message:
Terminal window
2024-07-09T05:30:33.583 INFO --- [et.reactor-4] l.s.i.p.handler : Request for service 'sqs' by principal 's3.amazonaws.com' for operation 'SendMessage' denied.
2024-07-09T05:30:33.583 DEBUG --- [et.reactor-4] l.s.i.p.handler : Necessary permissions for this action: ["Action 'sqs:SendMessage' for 'arn:aws:sqs:us-east-1:000000000000:s3-event-notification-queue'"]
2024-07-09T05:30:33.583 DEBUG --- [et.reactor-4] l.s.i.p.handler : 0 permissions have been explicitly denied: []
2024-07-09T05:30:33.583 DEBUG --- [et.reactor-4] l.s.i.p.handler : 0 permissions have been explicitly allowed: []
2024-07-09T05:30:33.583 DEBUG --- [et.reactor-4] l.s.i.p.handler : 1 permissions have been implicitly denied: ["Action 'sqs:SendMessage' for 'arn:aws:sqs:us-east-1:000000000000:s3-event-notification-queue'"]
Generate the IAM policy
Section titled “Generate the IAM policy”
Go to the IAM Policy Stream dashboard and review the API calls such as PutObject, SendMessage, and ReceiveMessage.
Notice that the SendMessage call was denied due to an IAM violation.
Click on the SQS.SendMessage action to see the suggested IAM policy.
LocalStack automatically recommends a resource-based policy for the SQS queue arn:aws:sqs:us-east-1:000000000000:s3-event-notification-queue.
Copy this policy and incorporate it into your Terraform configuration under the aws_sqs_queue resource by adding the policy attribute:
resource "aws_sqs_queue" "queue" {
name = "s3-event-notification-queue"
policy = <<POLICY
{
"Version": "2012-10-17",
"Statement": [
{
"Sid": "Test22bf6867",
"Effect": "Allow",
"Action": "sqs:SendMessage",
"Resource": "arn:aws:sqs:us-east-1:000000000000:s3-event-notification-queue",
"Principal": {
"Service": [
"s3.amazonaws.com"
]
},
"Condition": {
"ArnEquals": {
"aws:SourceArn": "arn:aws:s3:::s3-event-notification-bucket"
}
}
}
]
}
POLICY
}
Now, re-apply the Terraform configuration to update the SQS queue with the new policy:
Terminal window
lstk terraform apply
Next, trigger the event notification again by uploading a file to the S3 bucket.
You can confirm that the S3 bucket is correctly set up for event notifications through the SQS queue by checking if the message is received in the SQS queue:
Terminal window
lstk aws sqs receive-message \
--queue-url http://sqs.us-east-1.localhost.localstack.cloud:4566/000000000000/s3-event-notification-queue
The following output will show the message sent by the S3 bucket:
Terminal window
{
"Messages": [
{
"MessageId": "7c9d6b22-cb35-4a66-98dc-6f48dfc78f33",
"ReceiptHandle": "REDACTED",
"MD5OfBody": "10eacb105ec11badc56f7e0198e0c4ad",
"Body": "{\"Service\": \"Amazon S3\", \"Event\": \"s3:TestEvent\", \"Time\": \"2024-07-09T05:29:55.923Z\", \"Bucket\": \"s3-event-notification-bucket\", \"RequestId\": \"bfa882c0-a3b0-4549-b4c5-ac34167b3076\", \"HostId\": \"REDACTED\"}"
}
]
}
You can now check the IAM Policy Stream dashboard to confirm that there are no violations and that your AWS API requests have been successfully executed with the correct IAM policies.
Generate a comprehensive policy
Section titled “Generate a comprehensive policy”
In scenarios where there are many AWS services, and every AWS API request generates a policy it might be cumbersome to analyze every policy.
In such cases, you can generate one comprehensive policy for all your AWS resources together.
You can navigate to the Summary Policy tab on the IAM Policy Stream dashboard.
This concatenates the policy per principle which the policy should be attached to.
For the example above, you would be able to see the Identity Policy for the root user which has all the actions and resources inside one single policy file for the operations we performed.
On the other hand, you have the Resource Policy for the SQS queue, where you can see the permission necessary for the subscription.
For larger AWS applications, you would be able to find multiple roles and multiple resource-based policies depending on your scenario.
Testing the application
Section titled “Testing the application”
This section demonstrates how to test your IAM policies and verify both deny and allow scenarios using LocalStack’s IAM enforcement.
Testing Scenario 1: Deny (Without IAM Policy)
Section titled “Testing Scenario 1: Deny (Without IAM Policy)”
When you first upload a file to the S3 bucket without the proper SQS queue policy in place, S3 has no permission to send messages to the SQS queue, and the violation is reported.
Upload a test file:
Terminal window
echo "Test file content" > test-file.log
lstk aws s3 cp test-file.log s3://s3-event-notification-bucket/
Expected output - IAM Violation in LocalStack logs:
Terminal window
2024-07-09T05:30:33.583 INFO --- [et.reactor-4] l.s.i.p.handler : Request for service 'sqs' by principal 's3.amazonaws.com' for operation 'SendMessage' denied.
2024-07-09T05:30:33.583 DEBUG --- [et.reactor-4] l.s.i.p.handler : Necessary permissions for this action: ["Action 'sqs:SendMessage' for 'arn:aws:sqs:us-east-1:000000000000:s3-event-notification-queue'"]
2024-07-09T05:30:33.583 DEBUG --- [et.reactor-4] l.s.i.p.handler : 0 permissions have been explicitly denied: []
2024-07-09T05:30:33.583 DEBUG --- [et.reactor-4] l.s.i.p.handler : 0 permissions have been explicitly allowed: []
2024-07-09T05:30:33.583 DEBUG --- [et.reactor-4] l.s.i.p.handler : 1 permissions have been implicitly denied: ["Action 'sqs:SendMessage' for 'arn:aws:sqs:us-east-1:000000000000:s3-event-notification-queue'"]
IAM Policy Stream Dashboard showing the violation:
The dashboard clearly shows:
Action: SQS.SendMessage
Status: Denied (shown in red)
Principal: s3.amazonaws.com
Resource: arn:aws:sqs:us-east-1:000000000000:s3-event-notification-queue
Attempting to receive messages from the queue:
Terminal window
lstk aws sqs receive-message \
--queue-url http://sqs.us-east-1.localhost.localstack.cloud:4566/000000000000/s3-event-notification-queue
Expected output - the message is still delivered, because soft mode does not block the call:
{
"Messages": [
{
"MessageId": "5da627c5-5b4b-4202-a499-510222727e43",
"ReceiptHandle": "REDACTED",
"MD5OfBody": "dee5cf145a0678a0ac02e3b38aa302f7",
"Body": "{\"Records\": [{\"eventVersion\": \"2.1\", \"eventSource\": \"aws:s3\", \"awsRegion\": \"us-east-1\", \"eventName\": \"ObjectCreated:Put\", \"s3\": {\"bucket\": {\"name\": \"s3-event-notification-bucket\"}, \"object\": {\"key\": \"test-file.log\", \"size\": 18}}}]}"
}
]
}
In a production environment, where the same policy gap would be enforced by real AWS IAM, this SendMessage call would fail and the message would never arrive.
Testing Scenario 2: Allow (With IAM Policy)
Section titled “Testing Scenario 2: Allow (With IAM Policy)”
After applying the IAM policy generated by the Policy Stream to your SQS queue, the S3 service will be granted permission to send messages.
The required policy (already applied via Terraform):
{
"Version": "2012-10-17",
"Statement": [
{
"Sid": "Test22bf6867",
"Effect": "Allow",
"Action": "sqs:SendMessage",
"Resource": "arn:aws:sqs:us-east-1:000000000000:s3-event-notification-queue",
"Principal": {
"Service": [
"s3.amazonaws.com"
]
},
"Condition": {
"ArnEquals": {
"aws:SourceArn": "arn:aws:s3:::s3-event-notification-bucket"
}
}
}
]
}
Upload another test file:
Terminal window
echo "Test file with policy" > test-file-2.log
lstk aws s3 cp test-file-2.log s3://s3-event-notification-bucket/
Expected output - Success (no IAM violation):
Terminal window
upload: ./test-file-2.log to s3://s3-event-notification-bucket/test-file-2.log
LocalStack logs:
An allowed request produces no output from the IAM policy handler — only denials are logged.
Terminal window
lstk logs | grep "i.p.handler"
Only the entries from the earlier, un-permitted upload should remain.
IAM Policy Stream Dashboard showing no violations:
The dashboard shows all actions with green checkmarks, indicating successful execution.
Receive the message from the queue:
Terminal window
lstk aws sqs receive-message \
--queue-url http://sqs.us-east-1.localhost.localstack.cloud:4566/000000000000/s3-event-notification-queue
Expected output - Message successfully received:
{
"Messages": [
{
"MessageId": "7c9d6b22-cb35-4a66-98dc-6f48dfc78f33",
"ReceiptHandle": "REDACTED",
"MD5OfBody": "10eacb105ec11badc56f7e0198e0c4ad",
"Body": "{\"Service\": \"Amazon S3\", \"Event\": \"s3:TestEvent\", \"Time\": \"2024-07-09T05:29:55.923Z\", \"Bucket\": \"s3-event-notification-bucket\", \"RequestId\": \"bfa882c0-a3b0-4549-b4c5-ac34167b3076\", \"HostId\": \"REDACTED\"}"
}
]
}
The message body contains the S3 event notification with details about the uploaded file, confirming that the IAM policy is working correctly.
Verification Checklist
Section titled “Verification Checklist”
To ensure your IAM policies are correctly configured:
No IAM violations appear in the IAM Policy Stream dashboard
Messages are successfully delivered to the SQS queue
No new violation entries are logged for the SendMessage operation after the policy is applied
All API calls display green checkmarks in the Policy Stream dashboard
Conclusion
Section titled “Conclusion”
IAM Policy Stream streamlines your development process by minimizing the manual creation of policies and confirming the necessity of granted permissions.
However, it is advisable to manually confirm that your policy aligns with your intended actions.
Your code may unintentionally make requests, and LocalStack considers all requests made during policy generation as valid.
A practical scenario is automating tests, such as integration or end-to-end testing, against your application using LocalStack.
This setup allows LocalStack to automatically generate policies with the required permissions.
However, it’s important to note that these generated policies may not cover all possible requests, as only the requests made during testing are included.
You can then review and customize the policies to meet your needs, ensuring that overly permissive policies don’t find their way into production environments.

It’s important to find a balance, avoiding giving too many permissions while making sure the right ones are granted.
This challenge becomes more complex when dealing with AWS services that make requests not directly visible to users.
For instance, if an SNS topic sends a message to an SQS queue and the underlying call fails, there might be no clear error message, causing confusion, especially for those less familiar with the services.
IAM Policy Stream simplifies this by automatically generating the needed policies and showing them to users.
This makes it easier to integrate with resources, roles, and users, streamlining the development process.
Additionally, it serves as a useful learning tool, helping users understand the permissions linked to various AWS calls and improving the onboarding experience for newcomers to AWS.
Prerequisites
Section titled “Prerequisites”
lstk with LOCALSTACK_AUTH_TOKEN
Docker
Terraform & lstk terraform
AWS CLI with lstk aws
LocalStack account
jq
Architecture diagram
Section titled “Architecture diagram”
The following diagram illustrates the architecture of this tutorial:
In this architecture:
An S3 bucket is configured to send event notifications when objects are created
An SQS queue receives these notifications
The IAM Enforcement Engine intercepts API calls and checks for proper permissions
The IAM Policy Stream Dashboard captures all API requests and generates the necessary IAM policies
When a file is uploaded to the S3 bucket, S3 attempts to send a message to SQS, which initially fails due to missing permissions
The IAM Policy Stream automatically generates the required policy, which can then be applied to resolve the violation
Tutorial: Configure an S3 bucket for event notifications using SQS
Section titled “Tutorial: Configure an S3 bucket for event notifications using SQS”
In this tutorial, you will configure a LocalStack S3 bucket to send event notifications to an SQS queue.
You will then use IAM Policy Stream to generate the necessary IAM policy for the SQS queue.
You will use Terraform to create the resources and the AWS CLI to interact with them.
With LocalStack’s IAM enforcement enabled, you can thoroughly test your policy and ensure that the development setup mirrors the production environment.
Start your LocalStack container
Section titled “Start your LocalStack container”
Launch the LocalStack container on your local machine using the specified command:
Terminal window
LOCALSTACK_DEBUG=1 LOCALSTACK_IAM_SOFT_MODE=1 lstk start
In the above command:
LOCALSTACK_DEBUG=1 turns on detailed logging to check API calls and IAM violations.
LOCALSTACK_IAM_SOFT_MODE=1 lets you test IAM enforcement by logging violations without stopping the API calls.
Create the Terraform configuration
Section titled “Create the Terraform configuration”
Create a new file called main.tf for the Terraform setup of an S3 bucket and an SQS queue.
Start by using the aws_sqs_queue resource to create an SQS queue named s3-event-notification-queue.
resource "aws_sqs_queue" "queue" {
name = "s3-event-notification-queue"
}
Next, use the aws_s3_bucket resource to create an S3 bucket called s3-event-notification-bucket.
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "bucket" {
bucket = "s3-event-notification-bucket"
}
Finally, use the aws_s3_bucket_notification resource to link the S3 bucket with the SQS queue for sending notifications:
resource "aws_s3_bucket_notification" "bucket_notification" {
bucket = aws_s3_bucket.bucket.id
queue {
queue_arn = aws_sqs_queue.queue.arn
events = ["s3:ObjectCreated:*"]
}
}
Deploy the Terraform configuration
Section titled “Deploy the Terraform configuration”
You can use lstk terraform to deploy your Terraform configuration within the LocalStack environment.
Run the following commands to initialize and apply the Terraform configuration:
Terminal window
lstk terraform init
lstk terraform apply
You will be prompted to confirm the changes.
Type yes to continue.
Since LocalStack is used, no real AWS resources are created.
LocalStack will emulate ephemeral development resources that will be removed automatically once you stop the LocalStack container.
After applying the Terraform configuration, the output will appear similar to this:
Terminal window
aws_sqs_queue.queue: Creating...
aws_s3_bucket.bucket: Creating...
aws_s3_bucket.bucket: Creation complete after 1s [id=s3-event-notification-bucket]
aws_sqs_queue.queue: Still creating... [10s elapsed]
aws_sqs_queue.queue: Still creating... [20s elapsed]
aws_sqs_queue.queue: Creation complete after 26s [id=http://sqs.us-east-1.localhost.localstack.cloud:4566/000000000000/s3-event-notification-queue]
aws_s3_bucket_notification.bucket_notification: Creating...
aws_s3_bucket_notification.bucket_notification: Creation complete after 0s [id=s3-event-notification-bucket]
Apply complete! Resources: 3 added, 0 changed, 0 destroyed.
Start the IAM Policy Stream
Section titled “Start the IAM Policy Stream”
Access the LocalStack Web Application and go to the IAM Policy Stream dashboard.
This feature enables you to directly examine the generated policies, displaying the precise permissions required for each API call.
You’ll observe the Stream active status icon, indicating that making any local AWS API request will trigger the generation of an IAM Policy.
Now, let’s proceed to upload a file to the S3 bucket to trigger the event notification and generate the IAM policy.
Trigger the event notification
Section titled “Trigger the event notification”
Create a new file named some-log-file.log and upload it to the S3 bucket using the AWS CLI:
Terminal window
echo "Hello, LocalStack" > some-log-file.log
lstk aws s3 cp some-log-file.log s3://s3-event-notification-bucket/
Uploading a file will activate an event notification, sending a message to the SQS queue.
However, since the SQS queue lacks the necessary permissions, an IAM violation will appear in the IAM Policy Stream dashboard.
You can also navigate to the LocalStack logs and observe the IAM violation message:
Terminal window
2024-07-09T05:30:33.583 INFO --- [et.reactor-4] l.s.i.p.handler : Request for service 'sqs' by principal 's3.amazonaws.com' for operation 'SendMessage' denied.
2024-07-09T05:30:33.583 DEBUG --- [et.reactor-4] l.s.i.p.handler : Necessary permissions for this action: ["Action 'sqs:SendMessage' for 'arn:aws:sqs:us-east-1:000000000000:s3-event-notification-queue'"]
2024-07-09T05:30:33.583 DEBUG --- [et.reactor-4] l.s.i.p.handler : 0 permissions have been explicitly denied: []
2024-07-09T05:30:33.583 DEBUG --- [et.reactor-4] l.s.i.p.handler : 0 permissions have been explicitly allowed: []
2024-07-09T05:30:33.583 DEBUG --- [et.reactor-4] l.s.i.p.handler : 1 permissions have been implicitly denied: ["Action 'sqs:SendMessage' for 'arn:aws:sqs:us-east-1:000000000000:s3-event-notification-queue'"]
Generate the IAM policy
Section titled “Generate the IAM policy”
Go to the IAM Policy Stream dashboard and review the API calls such as PutObject, SendMessage, and ReceiveMessage.
Notice that the SendMessage call was denied due to an IAM violation.
Click on the SQS.SendMessage action to see the suggested IAM policy.
LocalStack automatically recommends a resource-based policy for the SQS queue arn:aws:sqs:us-east-1:000000000000:s3-event-notification-queue.
Copy this policy and incorporate it into your Terraform configuration under the aws_sqs_queue resource by adding the policy attribute:
resource "aws_sqs_queue" "queue" {
name = "s3-event-notification-queue"
policy = <<POLICY
{
"Version": "2012-10-17",
"Statement": [
{
"Sid": "Test22bf6867",
"Effect": "Allow",
"Action": "sqs:SendMessage",
"Resource": "arn:aws:sqs:us-east-1:000000000000:s3-event-notification-queue",
"Principal": {
"Service": [
"s3.amazonaws.com"
]
},
"Condition": {
"ArnEquals": {
"aws:SourceArn": "arn:aws:s3:::s3-event-notification-bucket"
}
}
}
]
}
POLICY
}
Now, re-apply the Terraform configuration to update the SQS queue with the new policy:
Terminal window
lstk terraform apply
Next, trigger the event notification again by uploading a file to the S3 bucket.
You can confirm that the S3 bucket is correctly set up for event notifications through the SQS queue by checking if the message is received in the SQS queue:
Terminal window
lstk aws sqs receive-message \
--queue-url http://sqs.us-east-1.localhost.localstack.cloud:4566/000000000000/s3-event-notification-queue
The following output will show the message sent by the S3 bucket:
Terminal window

You can now check the IAM Policy Stream dashboard to confirm that there are no violations and that your AWS API requests have been successfully executed with the correct IAM policies.
Generate a comprehensive policy
Section titled “Generate a comprehensive policy”
In scenarios where there are many AWS services, and every AWS API request generates a policy it might be cumbersome to analyze every policy.
In such cases, you can generate one comprehensive policy for all your AWS resources together.
You can navigate to the Summary Policy tab on the IAM Policy Stream dashboard.
This concatenates the policy per principle which the policy should be attached to.
For the example above, you would be able to see the Identity Policy for the root user which has all the actions and resources inside one single policy file for the operations we performed.
On the other hand, you have the Resource Policy for the SQS queue, where you can see the permission necessary for the subscription.
For larger AWS applications, you would be able to find multiple roles and multiple resource-based policies depending on your scenario.
Testing the application
Section titled “Testing the application”
This section demonstrates how to test your IAM policies and verify both deny and allow scenarios using LocalStack’s IAM enforcement.
Testing Scenario 1: Deny (Without IAM Policy)
Section titled “Testing Scenario 1: Deny (Without IAM Policy)”
When you first upload a file to the S3 bucket without the proper SQS queue policy in place, S3 has no permission to send messages to the SQS queue, and the violation is reported.
Upload a test file:
Terminal window
echo "Test file content" > test-file.log
lstk aws s3 cp test-file.log s3://s3-event-notification-bucket/

Testing Scenario 2: Allow (With IAM Policy)
Section titled “Testing Scenario 2: Allow (With IAM Policy)”
After applying the IAM policy generated by the Policy Stream to your SQS queue, the S3 service will be granted permission to send messages.
The required policy (already applied via Terraform):

"Version": "2012-10-17",
"Statement": [
{
"Sid": "Test22bf6867",
"Effect": "Allow",
"Action": "sqs:SendMessage",
"Resource": "arn:aws:sqs:us-east-1:000000000000:s3-event-notification-queue",
"Principal": {
"Service": [
"s3.amazonaws.com"
]
},
"Condition": {
"ArnEquals": {
"aws:SourceArn": "arn:aws:s3:::s3-event-notification-bucket"
}
}
}
]
}
Upload another test file:
Terminal window

lstk aws s3 cp test-file-2.log s3://s3-event-notification-bucket/
Expected output - Success (no IAM violation):
Terminal window

LocalStack logs:

The dashboard shows all actions with green checkmarks, indicating successful execution.
Receive the message from the queue:

--queue-url http://sqs.us-east-1.localhost.localstack.cloud:4566/000000000000/s3-event-notification-queue

}
]
}
The message body contains the S3 event notification with details about the uploaded file, confirming that the IAM policy is working correctly.
Verification Checklist
Section titled “Verification Checklist”
To ensure your IAM policies are correctly configured:
No IAM violations appear in the IAM Policy Stream dashboard
Messages are successfully delivered to the SQS queue
No new violation entries are logged for the SendMessage operation after the policy is applied
All API calls display green checkmarks in the Policy Stream dashboard
Conclusion
Section titled “Conclusion”
IAM Policy Stream streamlines your development process by minimizing the manual creation of policies and confirming the necessity of granted permissions.
However, it is advisable to manually confirm that your policy aligns with your intended actions.
Your code may unintentionally make requests, and LocalStack considers all requests made during policy generation as valid.
A practical scenario is automating tests, such as integration or end-to-end testing, against your application using LocalStack.
This setup allows LocalStack to automatically generate policies with the required permissions.
However, it’s important to note that these generated policies may not cover all possible requests, as only the requests made during testing are included.
You can then review and customize the policies to meet your needs, ensuring that overly permissive policies don’t find their way into production environments.

[PostgreSQL MERGE](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/sql-merge.html)
    34	- Compute the retirement numerator and denominator on the same protected pre-apply inventory view. Row locks protect existing IDs, while new frames and edits that move into or out of scope require a shared writer protocol. Start with a transaction-scoped inventory lock held in shared mode by manual writes and DELTA applies, and in exclusive mode by snapshots. Take per-frame locks in stable ID order. This serializes promotion of snapshots even when their scopes are disjoint. Keep it out of upload, parsing, and staging. Measure lock time before enabling the feature. Never infer absence from a partial stream or an unrecoverable CSV parse error. Decide whether unidentifiable rows, scope violations, and header-only snapshots fail the whole job. The proposed default is to fail a snapshot before any inventory write when a safety check fails.
    35	
    36	### Snapshot watermark
    37	
    38	- Persist snapshot_as_of on the job. Accept a producer-supplied export watermark at job creation. When omitted, derive it from MAX(modified_date) after scanning the complete file. Use one documented source timezone and precision for comparisons. Require the exporter to supply an explicit watermark when the file cannot establish one. MAX(modified_date) measures the newest row change and can lag the time a complete export was generated. It also cannot prove completeness, so prefer the explicit export watermark for feeds where these times differ.
    39	- Use canonical scope keys in a containment hierarchy: GLOBAL, country, country/region, and country/region/environment. Require a region for every environment-level FULL_SNAPSHOT in the first release. Reject a country/environment scope such as UK/UNDERGROUND at job creation. An operator can export a separate authoritative snapshot for each region or use DELTA for a cross-region file.
    40	- Before inventory writes and under the snapshot apply lock, reject a watermark outside the freshness window (proposed default 24 hours), in the future beyond allowed clock skew, or strictly below the maximum committed watermark for the requested scope and its ancestors. Equal watermarks pass this check. On successful commit, advance only the requested scope's watermark, including when the job completes with row errors. A failed job leaves all watermarks as they were.
    41	- A newer descendant watermark does not reject an enclosing snapshot. Apply normal row conflict checks throughout the requested scope, including newer child scopes. Before retiring absent frames, exclude the entire subtree of each descendant whose committed watermark is strictly newer than the incoming watermark. Report the protected scopes and skipped retirement count. A descendant at the same watermark remains eligible. For example, a GLOBAL export at 11:30 can apply after a partition snapshot at 12:00, with retirement excluded in that partition. A partition export at 11:00 fails if an ancestor already committed at 12:00.
    42	- Among the remaining absent active frames, exclude any whose current valid_from or source_modified_at is after snapshot_as_of and record SKIPPED_RETIREMENT_NEWER_THAN_SNAPSHOT. This protects newer current versions, including edits within the same scope. Count only eligible retirements in the 10% numerator and keep the denominator as all pre-apply active frames in the declared scope. Capture the watermark checks, both exclusion counts, the breaker calculation, and the scope watermark update in the same protected apply transaction.
    43	
    44	### Snapshot history and reactivation
    45	
    46	The agreed representation is a new current version with status RETIRED and reason MISSING_FROM_FULL_SNAPSHOT. Define how current inventory queries treat that version and how a later import reactivates it. Existing manual deletion closes the last current version without opening a replacement. Keep those behaviors explicit in the status and history contract. If snapshot closure sets closed_by_change_source, extend the V2 constraint, which currently allows only MANUAL_DELETE. [V2 migration](../../src/backend/src/main/resources/db/migration/V2__add_frame_change_source.sql)
    47	
    48	## Goals and non-goals
    49	
    50	- Deliver authenticated upload, visible job progress and row errors, retry-safe imports, audited versions, scoped retirement, and transactional outbox records.
    51	- Leave mass deletion, generalized CSV mapping, automatic repair of malformed source values, and multi-scope FULL_SNAPSHOT uploads outside the first release. If authoritative cross-region exports become a regular need, consider one atomic job over explicitly named scopes, each with its own watermark and retirement check.
    52	
    53	## Alternatives weighed
    54	
    55	- Keep the S3-to-Lambda bridge as requested. Direct S3-to-SQS delivery could remove an operational failure path if the bridge only forwards events. Verify what routing or event normalization the Lambda needs to own.
    56	- Keep UNLOGGED staging with full source replay for initial implementation. Durable staging could reduce replay cost and operational complexity after failover, at the cost of logging intermediate data. Benchmark with the expected maximum file.
    57	- Reuse versioned history as the initial design direction. Add a separate frame_history table only if it serves a distinct audited need. Otherwise two history stores would require agreement on which is authoritative.
    58	
    59	## Key decisions and implementation sequence
    60	
    61	1. Map the CSV to the current schema and the proposed six entities. Resolve source timestamp parsing, manual-edit ordering, force authorization, link semantics, duplicate IDs, and schema ownership before migrations.
    62	2. Add durable job, row error, lineage, and outbox storage through additive Flyway migrations. Expose BFF job creation and status, including counts, fatal errors, and paginated row errors. Set upload-size, row-count, timeout, and retention limits from the agreed operating envelope.
    63	3. Implement the S3 event bridge, SQS dispatch and DLQ, and Temporal start. Exercise duplicate notifications, late events, ambiguous starts, and reconciliation before applying inventory.
    64	4. Implement staging and atomic DELTA apply. Run the supplied CSV against PostgreSQL 18 and check replay, timestamp collisions, manual edits, forced overwrite, malformed quoting, duplicate IDs, lost staging, and worker failure immediately after commit.
    65	5. Add scoped FULL_SNAPSHOT with a protected retirement calculation. Verify that malformed rows with IDs stay present, out-of-scope frames stay untouched, and the exact 5% and 10% boundaries behave as agreed. Exercise rejection of environment scopes without a region, expired and out-of-order watermarks, watermark equality, derived watermarks, newer ancestors rejecting narrower snapshots, newer descendants protecting entire subtrees while present rows still upsert, frames created or moved into scope after export, and concurrent manual writes. Roll out DELTA first, then enable snapshot after observing apply times and reviewing operator safeguards.
    66	6. Track queue age and DLQ depth, time in each job state, staging retries, apply transaction duration, row error codes, retirement guard trips, and outbox lag. Correlate logs by job ID and keep presigned URLs and raw row content out of logs.
9:Inventory operators can upload `inventory_frame.csv` from the running application and see the result as the job progresses. A routine update changes only the frames named in the file. An authoritative snapshot can also retire missing frames within a declared area of the inventory. Every accepted change is visible in frame history.
19:- Support `FULL_SNAPSHOT` for a single declared scope. Require country and region for environment-level scopes. Protect frames present in malformed rows, frames changed after the export watermark, and partitions with newer snapshots. Prevent retirement when the malformed-row rate exceeds 5% and abort before inventory writes if more than 10% of scoped active frames would retire.
26:- A single snapshot covering several separately named scopes in the first release. Operators can submit separate regional snapshots or use `DELTA` for a cross-region update.
41:The job creation API takes the import mode, optional snapshot scope and export watermark, and explicit force flag. Spring Boot validates the requested scope and permissions, creates an AWAITING_UPLOAD job, and returns its ID and the presigned PUT details through the BFF. The upload key is uploads/{jobId}/inventory_frame.csv. Use a create-only PUT and persist the accepted S3 object version so all retries read the same bytes. Expose job status, counts, fatal errors, and paginated row errors through the BFF.
43:Configure S3 to send object-created notifications for the uploads/ prefix directly to a standard SQS queue in the same AWS Region. Grant the bucket permission to publish through a queue policy scoped to the bucket ARN and owner account. The Spring Boot consumer handles the native S3 notification envelope, recognizes the S3 test event, and processes each object record. It decodes the key and verifies the bucket, key, object version, and size, then conditionally records PENDING and starts Temporal workflow csv-import-{jobId}. Duplicate or out-of-order records must preserve the existing object binding and job state. Acknowledge the message after each applicable record has been handled, including confirming successful or already-completed workflow dispatch. If processing a later record fails, replay of earlier records uses the same job and workflow identities. Retry with backoff. Before a DLQ event can fail a job, reconcile ambiguous workflow starts and check that the job is still dispatchable. Reconcile old AWAITING_UPLOAD and PENDING jobs against S3 and Temporal.
51:The Temporal worker reads the pinned object and streams logical CSV records into job- and attempt-scoped UNLOGGED staging. Heartbeats report progress and let the worker detect cancellation. Keep the EOF completion marker in the same unlogged storage as the data. Before apply, check the marker and staged counts. If a crash leaves staging incomplete or empty, reload from S3. Store row errors with stable job, row, and error keys for retries. Track identifiable frame IDs independently of row validity. Hash canonical typed frame values with SHA-256 over a versioned, ordered encoding. Preserve meaningful text, normalize typed numeric values by value, encode null distinctly, order external references by type, and preserve the position of links. Exclude job metadata, version validity, and source timestamps from the payload hash. Compare hashes using the same encoding version. After staging, reject every row for a frame ID that appears more than once, report DUPLICATE_FRAME_ID for each duplicate row, and keep the ID in the snapshot presence set. Count each rejected logical record once toward the malformed-row threshold, even if it has several validation errors.
55:Use the existing frame table for stable identity and frame_version for current and historical values. Resolve region, town, postcode, and format through existing lookup tables. Attach external references and ordered links to the resulting frame version. Add job, row error, scope watermark, and import lineage storage through Flyway. Map the complete CSV to the existing model, including site and spec fields on frame_version. The BFF, protobuf service definitions, Spring service, and worker need changes for job creation, progress, and application.
61:Promote a complete staging attempt in one transaction. Acquire the job lock and verify eligibility before writing. Use one source candidate per target key and MERGE RETURNING where it fits. Close current versions and append replacements in separate set-based statements. Commit inventory, versioned references and links, the applicable scope watermark, and job result together. If the worker loses the commit response, return the stored result when it retries.
65:Keep staging outside the inventory lock. During promotion, take a shared transaction-scoped inventory lock for manual writes and DELTA and an exclusive lock for FULL_SNAPSHOT. Obtain frame locks in stable ID order. Evaluate scope membership, watermark checks, and retirement against the protected pre-apply view.
67:Require scope to be GLOBAL or a canonical country, country/region, or country/region/environment path. Use the explicit snapshot_as_of where available, otherwise derive it from MAX(modified_date) on the complete file. Check freshness and reject watermarks below the greatest committed value for the scope or its ancestors. A broader snapshot can still apply its present rows under the ordinary conflict rules when a descendant has a newer watermark. Protect that entire descendant subtree from retirement.
69:Before writing inventory, fail the entire snapshot for a header-only file, an incomplete export, or an unrecoverable CSV parse error. Also fail the snapshot if any row has no recoverable frame ID or any record is outside the declared scope. Keep job diagnostics and leave inventory and the scope watermark unchanged. Count any identifiable frame ID in the CSV as present, including when other fields are malformed. Among absent active frames, exclude protected child scopes and current versions whose valid_from or source_modified_at exceeds the export watermark. Record SKIPPED_RETIREMENT_NEWER_THAN_SNAPSHOT for the latter. If eligible retirements exceed 10% of all active frames in the declared scope, fail before inventory writes. If more than 5% of CSV rows are malformed, fail the entire snapshot before writing inventory. Keep the job diagnostics and leave the scope watermark unadvanced. Represent each accepted retirement with a new RETIRED version and MISSING_FROM_FULL_SNAPSHOT. Advance only the incoming scope watermark on a successful commit.
71:Exclude snapshot-retired frames from the default inventory list. Expose them through an explicit retired filter, direct lookup, and frame history.
109:   - Create `inventoryimport/ImportDispatch.java` to decode the S3 envelope, handle test events, reconcile stale jobs, start Temporal idempotently, and handle DLQ outcomes without regressing running or completed jobs. Keep queue acknowledgment at the message boundary.
110:   - Create `inventoryimport/CsvImportWorkflow.java` and `inventoryimport/CsvImportActivities.java` to sequence staging and promotion, configure bounded retries and heartbeats, and record terminal failures. Register the dispatcher and worker through `inventoryimport/ImportConfiguration.java` so the application can run without AWS/Temporal import wiring when imports are disabled.
112:   - Create `inventoryimport/ImportApplyRepository.java` for the set-based transaction and eligibility checks. Reserve stable IDs, lock them in order, and re-read current versions before evaluating the timestamp/hash rules. Resolve existing dimensions, close and append versions, copy or replace versioned children as appropriate, and persist the final job outcome with the inventory changes. Measure guards before mutation, including scope completeness, empty snapshots, malformed percentage, watermark checks, and retirement percentage.
129:   - Create backend tests under `src/backend/src/test/java/com/global/ct/frameinventory/inventoryimport/`. Use `InventoryCsvReaderTests.java` for the supplied CSV, multiline fields, empty files, missing IDs, duplicate IDs, exact byte and logical-row limits, hash stability, and UTC timestamp parsing under non-UTC JVM and database session settings. Use `ImportDispatchTests.java` for native envelopes, test events, duplicates, delayed delivery, and ambiguous starts followed by DLQ. Use `ImportApplyTests.java` with PostgreSQL 18 for the full apply transaction, idempotent retries, legacy and manual edits, force restoration, reactivation, and rollback without inventory or watermark changes. Exercise stale, equal, enclosing, and descendant watermarks, the exact 5% and 10% boundaries, concurrent manual writes, incomplete staging, and activity retry after commit.

Completed the Inventive Catalyst review. Read the entire design and all 21 context files, including all 1,000 CSV records and the visible text from the saved LocalStack page. No reads were missing and no files were changed.

- **Major — Snapshot completeness.** A clean file missing 50 of 1,000 frames can pass parsing, scope validation, and both percentage checks, then incorrectly retire those 50 frames. Require trusted exporter metadata that binds the scope, export time, expected row count, and digest to the accepted upload. Keep ordinary uploads on `DELTA`. This requires exporter integration and makes snapshot availability dependent on that integration. [Design](/Users/alexcallow/Sites/frame-inventory-exercise-main/docs/designs/bulk-csv-inventory-import-design.md:67) · [Source RFC](/Users/alexcallow/Sites/frame-inventory-exercise-main/docs/designs/bulk-csv-inventory-import.md:38)
- **Major — Snapshot promotion work.** The input cap leaves the number of retirements under the global write lock unbounded. In a scope with one million active frames, 900,000 protected by newer child snapshots and 1,000 present in the upload, the remaining 99,000 frames can be retired within the 10% threshold. Define an initial workload and transaction budget, and measure writer wait on a representative inventory. This can require oversized scopes to be submitted separately and requires timeout handling that preserves job diagnostics. [Design](/Users/alexcallow/Sites/frame-inventory-exercise-main/docs/designs/bulk-csv-inventory-import-design.md:65)
